To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Milwaukee's urban retail system in the nineteenth century developed a spatial hierarchy with a central business district, a number of smaller shopping districts, and a dispersed pattern in which retail outlets were located throughout the city.

(1) the number of retail outlets in Milwaukee grew rapidly in the nineteenth century, especially after 1860; (2) retail outlets were dispersed in the city and were found in all parts of the city, including those far from the central business district; (3) there was a high degree of clustering of retail outlets, especially in the central business district, but also in other parts of the city; (4) the number of clusters increased rapidly in the nineteenth cen- tury,
(a) Milwaukee’s nineteenth-century retailing was spatially structured, (b) the structure changed over time and (c) the structure varied with the social and ethnic characteristics of neighbourhoods.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the geographical structure of nineteenth century urban retailing.
the spatial distribution of urban retailing in Milwaukee during the nineteenth century.

the following issues: 1) the degree to which retailing in Milwaukee was geographically concentrated or dispersed; 2) the functional character of the central business district (CBD); 3) the functional and spatial characteristics of non-central shopping clusters; and 4) the spatial structure and evolution of retailing in the pre-motor age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nineteenth-century American city had a retail system that was both more complex and more sophisticated than the simple, one-level central business district of the conventional model.

the spatial structure of urban retailing in the nineteenth-century city is a complex phenomenon, but that it is possible to identify a number of general patterns which are consistent with the evidence from Milwaukee.
the retail structure of Milwaukee in the second half, but not necessarily the first half, of the nineteenth century is consistent with the hypothesis of the existence of a central place hierarchy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
retailing in the nineteenth-century city was not only a function of the central business district, but was also a function of a number of shopping districts in the city.
the spatial distribution of retailing in the pre-urban era is not random and the spatial structure of the urban retail system is not random.
the spatial organization of nineteenth-century urban retail trade in Milwaukee was complex and dynamic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nineteenth-century retailing was not as simple as we have often been led to believe, and that the retailing of the past was more complex than the retailing of today.
the spatial distribution of urban retailing was more complex in the pre-motor age than is commonly supposed.
the spatial organization of retailing in the nineteenth-century city was much more complex than has previously been assumed.
